summary: Self-service 'Experiment Pod' automation for temporary research projects (Slack + Confluence + Jira)
description:
Issue summary:
We need an automated self-service workflow to provision temporary cross-product 'Experiment Pod' environments for short-lived research projects (hackathons, model eval sprints, partner pilots). Each pod should create a Jira project, a Confluence space, and a Slack channel set using centralized templates and enforced guardrails (retention, membership controls, audit hooks).

Motivation / Impact:
- Current manual provisioning is slow (0.5–2 business days) and error-prone; teams create inconsistent spaces and slack conventions.
- Research teams frequently spin up many short-lived projects; lacking lifecycle automation leads to stale spaces and audit headaches.
- Need to reduce ops overhead while ensuring compliance (retention, DLP hooks, and access approvals).

Background / Context:
- Similar ephemeral automation exists for some pods but is fragmented.
- Security wants approved groups and audit events for all created artifacts.
- Product & Research teams want a single button self-service flow in the internal portal with optional manager approval for enterprise pods.
request_details:
Desired features (high level):
1) Self-service form (internal portal) that captures: pod name, owning team, experiment lead, duration/TTL (1–90 days), access list or Okta group, and classification (public/internal/confidential).
2) Approval gate: instant for self_serve TTL <= 7 days and < 10 users; manager approval required otherwise.
3) Provisioning actions: create Jira project (kanban template, default workflows), Confluence space from sandbox template (pre-populated experiment checklist and retention metadata), and a Slack channel with naming convention and pinned onboarding message.
4) Lifecycle automation: automatic TTL enforcement with email notices at 7/3/1 day(s) before expiration, one-click extend, and automated archival/cleanup after expiry (with audit log).
5) Audit & telemetry: send creation/deletion/approval events to Datadog and write structured audit entries to the compliance Confluence page; capture service-account and webhook activity.
6) RBAC: integrate with Okta groups and centrally managed service accounts; created artifacts inherit group membership and use ephemeral service tokens.
7) Fail-safe: if any step fails, rollback created artifacts and notify requester + infra on-call with runbook link.
acceptance_criteria: Internal portal form that provisions Jira/Confluence/Slack with one submit
Approval flow works per TTL rules and logs approvals
TTL lifecycle notifications and archive job run automatically
Audit events emitted to Datadog and appended to compliance Confluence space
Rollback works on partial failure (no orphaned spaces/channels)
Documentation and runbook published to Confluence and linked in the portal
implementation_notes:
Proposed implementation approach:
- UI: add a short flow in the internal provisioning portal (Frontend Team) that POSTs a request to platform-automation service.
- Orchestration: platform-automation will call terraform-managed modules (or internal provisioning lambdas) for each system in a transactional way; use a saga pattern with compensating actions.
- Slack: use the internal Slack app (bot) to create channels, set retention tags, and post onboarding messages.
- Confluence & Jira: use Atlassian REST APIs with a central service account; leverage a namespaced template repo for space/project skeletons.
- Auth: use Okta group lookups and SCIM to sync membership; create ephemeral service tokens stored in HashiCorp Vault.
- Observability: emit structured events (payload includes key, owner, template, TTL, approval_id) to the events stream (Kafka) and Datadog.
- Tests: e2e test harness that runs a dry-provision without creating real artifacts (mock APIs) plus integration tests in staging region.
- Rollback: implement compensating calls that delete created artifacts and record failure reason to central incident log.
rollout_plan:
1) Prototype in staging: small group of research engineers (2 weeks).
2) User feedback loop and iterate on form fields & templates (1 week).
3) Soft launch to consenting teams with quota limits (2 weeks).
4) Full launch with automated TTL enforcement and documented runbook (GA).
5) Post-launch: monitor for 30 days for failure patterns; add rate limits and quota controls if needed.
risks:
- Atlassian API rate limits may cause partial failures; need retry/backoff strategy.
- Incorrect TTL handling could lead to premature deletion or excess retention; require conservative defaults.
- RBAC misconfiguration could expose confidential spaces; require automated policy validation and pre-launch security review.
- Slack app permission model needs least-privilege check; legal/infosec signoff required for posting user invites.
- Automation creating many artifacts could increase cost/metadata clutter if not pruned properly.
